display_name: Fritz Haag Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese, Mosel
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Sonnenuhr sundial sits on pure gray Devonian slate that tilts 60–70° toward the Mosel, giving Fritz Haag’s Auslese 90° noon sun in October while the river below bounces extra light back up. That extra hang-time lets botrytis concentrate berries down to 90–100° Oechsle without losing the 8–9 g/L racing acidity that keeps the wine levitating.",
  "wine_summary": "Fritz Haag has farmed the middle-Mosel since 1605; today Wilhelm Haag still refuses chaptalization even in cool years, so must-weight is earned solely by crop-level reduction and ultra-late picking. Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is a single 6 ha amphitheater of ungrafted Riesling rooted on blue slate; the 2018 Auslese hit 98° Oechsle and stopped fermentation at 7% abv with 92 g/L residual sugar, giving a wine that feels like candied grapefruit suspended on a tightwire of slate-driven salt and smoke. These wines routinely outlive their corks—2001s poured at the estate last year still showed lemon-meringue tension—and they cost half what comparable Spätlese or Auslese from the Rheingau or Nahe command.",
  "terroir_expression": "Devonian slate here is 400-million-year-old, mica-rich and friable, so roots plunge 8–12 m to find the water that keeps canopies green through Mosel’s 350 mm annual rainfall. The broken slate radiates heat overnight, extending ripening into cold October dawns; that diurnal swing locks in tartaric acid while concentrating quince and lime peel flavors. River reflection adds diffuse light, so even shaded berries ripen skins fully, yielding the translucent gold-green hue and the faint smoky struck-match note that signals blue slate.",
  "vinification_summary": "Whole-cluster pressing at 1.2 bar for three hours gives 55% yield; juice settles 24 h, then spontaneous fermentation in 1,000-L Mosel fuder stops on its own when alcohol hits 7% and sugar falls below 100 g/L—no sulfur until first racking, preserving the thiol-driven passion-fruit top note. The wine ages ten months on gross lees; batonnage is skipped so the yeast layer acts as oxygen buffer, polishing the acidity without adding cream.",

Prüm Graacher Himmelreich Auslese ($70) while offering more consistent botrytis spice. Worth it if you want 25-year Riesle for less than a dollar per year of aging.",

parsed.hook: The Sonnenuhr sundial sits on pure gray Devonian slate that tilts 60–70° toward the Mosel, giving Fritz Haag’s Auslese 90° noon sun in October while the river below bounces extra light back up. That extra hang-time lets botrytis concentrate berries down to 90–100° Oechsle without losing the 8–9 g/L racing acidity that keeps the wine levitating.
parsed.wine_summary: Fritz Haag has farmed the middle-Mosel since 1605; today Wilhelm Haag still refuses chaptalization even in cool years, so must-weight is earned solely by crop-level reduction and ultra-late picking. Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr is a single 6 ha amphitheater of ungrafted Riesling rooted on blue slate; the 2018 Auslese hit 98° Oechsle and stopped fermentation at 7% abv with 92 g/L residual sugar, giving a wine that feels like candied grapefruit suspended on a tightwire of slate-driven salt and smoke. These wines routinely outlive their corks—2001s poured at the estate last year still showed lemon-meringue tension—and they cost half what comparable Spätlese or Auslese from the Rheingau or Nahe command.
parsed.terroir_expression: Devonian slate here is 400-million-year-old, mica-rich and friable, so roots plunge 8–12 m to find the water that keeps canopies green through Mosel’s 350 mm annual rainfall. The broken slate radiates heat overnight, extending ripening into cold October dawns; that diurnal swing locks in tartaric acid while concentrating quince and lime peel flavors. River reflection adds diffuse light, so even shaded berries ripen skins fully, yielding the translucent gold-green hue and the faint smoky struck-match note that signals blue slate.
parsed.vinification_summary: Whole-cluster pressing at 1.2 bar for three hours gives 55% yield; juice settles 24 h, then spontaneous fermentation in 1,000-L Mosel fuder stops on its own when alcohol hits 7% and sugar falls below 100 g/L—no sulfur until first racking, preserving the thiol-driven passion-fruit top note. The wine ages ten months on gross lees; batonnage is skipped so the yeast layer acts as oxygen buffer, polishing the acidity without adding cream.
